extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of mathematics; mathematicians interested in foundations and pedagogy
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating foundations and pedagogy of analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical/historical assessment of competing foundational frameworks (constructivism, intuitionism, classical/non-standard analysis) with attention to pedagogical implications and standards for mathematical meaning. The page discusses criteria used by practitioners to judge acceptability, success, and pedagogical suitability of mathematical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Klein–Fraenkel criterion (success of infinitesimal theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory of infinitesimals is successful if one can prove a mean value theorem for arbitrary intervals, including infinitesimal ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originating with Klein (1908) and Fraenkel (1928); satisfied by the Hewitt–Loś–Robinson theory via the transfer principle (see Appendix A). Used as a concrete technical criterion for judging the adequacy of an infinitesimal continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical meaning (constructive requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical statements should have numerical meaning: if you say something exists you ought to be able to produce it; if you assert a function on the naturals, you ought to be able to produce a machine which calculates it for each number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop's central standard: existence must be witnessed by a construction (computability). Dependence on principles like LPO (limited principle of omniscience) or the law of excluded middle (LEM) undermines numerical meaning and is therefore rejected by Brouwer and Bishop. Feferman identifies LPO as a special case of LEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of LPO/LEM as a defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependence on the limited principle of omniscience (LPO) — e.g., 'it is possible to search a sequence of integers to see whether they all vanish' — or more generally on the law of excluded middle is a source of non-numerical (non-constructive) reasoning and is to be rejected in constructive mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works or constructions that rely on LPO/LEM (for example, typical constructions of Robinson-style infinitesimals are said to rely on LPO) are criticized for lacking numerical meaning. This is used as a foundational evaluative criterion by constructivists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of integers / finitely performable operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics should be concerned with finite operations on the integers; integers should be either concretely given or produced by a finite method (computable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop anchors his stance in a commitment he calls integr-ity: the primacy of integers and finite operations. He allows this primacy could be empirically overturned, but until then this serves as a foundational criterion for acceptable mathematics in his view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustability to increase numerical content
rubrics_metrics.description: A classical result is more acceptable if it can be adjusted to increase its numerical content (for example by strengthening hypotheses and/or weakening conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note that some classical analysis results can be modified this way (cf. Subsection 4.1). Bishop felt that such adjustment was not available for Robinson-style infinitesimals, which contributed to his rejection of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-constructivity at the basic number-system level is a fault
rubrics_metrics.description: If an approach (e.g., the hyperreal approach) incorporates an element of non-constructivity at the basic level of the very number system, this is a foundational defect from a constructivist standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion motivated Bishop's opposition to Robinson-style infinitesimals: an allegedly non-constructive number system is unacceptable because it undermines numerical meaning and computability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive epsilontic requirement (explicit rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive analysis requires epsilontic definitions that include explicit rates of convergence (e.g., a constructive Cauchy sequence specifies a rate), and replacement of epsilontics by infinitesimals threatens these constructive requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing Weierstrassian epsilontics by a theory of infinitesimals 'removes the bread and butter of constructive analysis' since constructive proofs rely on explicit rates; this is an evaluative standard for pedagogical and foundational acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical acceptability: reliance on teacher's authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods whose acceptance by students necessarily rests on trust in the teacher (for example acceptance of extension/transfer principles without constructive demonstration) are pedagogically suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesized pedagogical objection to non-standard analysis: the use of extension and transfer principles requires students to accept axiomatic machinery on authority rather than constructively understanding it. The authors argue this pedagogical objection does not fully explain Bishop's criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical pedagogical efficacy (evidence-based teaching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical judgments should take into account field studies and empirical data showing which methods better impart understanding (e.g., Sullivan's 1976 study showing infinitesimal approaches can be more successful than standard methods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors criticize Bishop for not addressing such empirical studies in his review; empirical success is presented as an important criterion for adopting teaching methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and explanation of axioms in teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing an axiomatic approach (e.g., Keisler's infinitesimal calculus), instructors/authors should explain the axioms rather than treating them as mere conveniences for generating proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop complained that Keisler 'has not explained the axioms' and that proofs generated by axioms whose intuitive content 'will certainly escape the students' are pedagogically unsatisfactory. This is used as a standard for evaluating textbooks and teaching materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency/integrity in publication (galley-proof additions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive additions made at the galley-proof stage that affect claims or tone (e.g., the 'debasement' paragraph added by Bishop) should be disclosed or footnoted to avoid misleading the reader about the original oral presentation and ensuing discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue the unacknowledged galley-stage insertion created an ethically problematic juxtaposition (vitriolic remark + absence of panel reaction) and recommend transparency to avoid misrepresenting reactions or consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial impartiality / conflict-of-interest avoidance in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and reviewers should avoid choices that create the appearance of bias or conflict (for example, choosing a reviewer whose known foundational stance strongly opposes the book's approach), and should be careful if editorial choices are motivated by sales or ideological goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halmos' editorial philosophy allowed reviewers to 'say (or imply) what he thinks' and to use reviews as a springboard for ideological agenda; the authors point to potential impropriety when editorial decisions intersect with personal involvement (e.g., translation efforts) and existing biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational coherence: acceptability of post-LEM numerical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A central evaluative question is whether post-LEM numerical meaning (mathematical meaning in the presence of the law of excluded middle) is mathematically coherent and acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bishop–Keisler controversy is framed around this dichotomy: constructivists question post-LEM numerical meaning, while classical mathematicians accept it. Answering this question is treated as decisive for judging the foundational legitimacy of approaches like non-standard analysis.
